                    ### Question
                    A 39-year-old man comes to the physician with a 4-week history of lesions on his penis and scrotum. He has no pain or discharge from the lesions. Two years ago, he was diagnosed with chronic myeloid leukemia and was treated with imatinib. He takes no medications. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years and drinks one to two beers on the weekends. He is sexually active and had unprotected intercourse with a woman about 4 months ago while abroad on business. He appears well. His temperature is 37°C (98°F), pulse is 85/min, and blood pressure is 128/82 mm Hg. Examination shows 3 nontender lesions up to 1 cm in size. A photograph of the lesions is shown. There is no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Treponema pallidum
opb. Klebsiella granulomatis
opc. Herpes simplex virus
opd. Haemophilus ducreyi
ope. Chlamydia trachomatis

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with nontender lesions on the penis and scrotum, which are characteristic of certain sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Treponema pallidum, the causative agent of syphilis, is known for causing painless genital lesions, making it a strong consideration given the patient's history of unprotected intercourse. While Klebsiella granulomatis (Calymmatobacterium granulomatis) can also cause painless genital ulcers (granuloma inguinale), the overall presentation and the context of potential syphilis exposure suggest Treponema pallidum is more likely. Other options, such as herpes simplex virus and Haemophilus ducreyi, are less likely due to the absence of painful symptoms, and Chlamydia trachomatis typically presents with discharge, which is not noted here. Therefore, the most likely causal organism is Treponema pallidum.
